newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Inventories data setback for Australia Q1 GDP.
newsitem.headline: Inventories data setback for Australia Q1 GDP.

text.p: Expectations of strong first quarter Australian economic growth received a setback on Thursday with the release of data showing that consumption, one of the key factors driving growth, may have actually worked to hold down the final growth figure.
After a poor December quarter, consumption rebounded strongly in the March quarter and it is expected to be a key contributor to first quarter growth domestic product (GDP).

But that same consumption has meant that firms have run down stock levels dramatically, possibly because they underestimated the strength of demand, which means that business stocks will now make a negative contribution to GDP, analysts said.
The level of business stocks, or inventories, fell by 2.1 percent in the March quarter.
This was well below median forecasts of a 0.5 percent rise, and the December quarter rise of 1.0 percent.
It was the first time the level of stocks has fallen since the September quarter of 1993.
"It's a case, with the stocks numbers, of being bad for historic growth but good for future growth," HSBC Markets economist Anthony Thompson said.

The change in the level of stocks feeds through to gross domestic product (GDP) calculations. When stock levels grow by less than in the previous quarter, or as in this case actually fall, it means they will detract from that quarter's growth.

"I think the important point though is that with a lot of sales having been met through stock rundowns, it's important to also look at spending, and that was certainly a lot stronger in the March quarter -- private spending we estimate was up 2.2
(percent)," ANZ Treasury economist David de Garis said.
Forecasts for GDP were being revised down from a median of around 1.1 percent, although quarterly balance of payments data on Friday is needed before final forecasts can be made.

"It was a bigger fall than we'd expected, but you can explain it as partly due to the increase in demand and partly due to the overhang in stocks from the previous quarter," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.
"GDP for the quarter now looks like coming in under one percent," he said.

But against that, if, as many economists think, the fall in stocks was due to the strong consumption demand and therefore could be considered involuntary, it augurs well for growth prospects later this year.

If business is confident of the stronger demand continuing, they will have to lift production to meet the demand and also to build back up stock levels, analysts said. This should then feed through to stronger overall economic growth.

"With inventories being run down a little it sets the groundwork for a pick-up later in this year, as as the economy picks up they will have to re-stock," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
"It's consistent with the view that the economy will have to be a little bit stronger," he said.

However, as stocks had been rising so strongly since their last fall, analysts said that it was possible businesses may allow stock levels to unwind further, meaning there was still potential for stocks to make a negative or weak GDP contribution next quarter as well.
